claim: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases play a role in regulating blood pressure.
source: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases play a role in many important facets of human physiology, from regulating blood pressure to intestinal fluid secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established role of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases.

claim: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases play a role in intestinal fluid secretion.
source: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases play a role in many important facets of human physiology, from regulating blood pressure to intestinal fluid secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established role of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of human GC-C in complex with Hsp90 and Cdc37 was determined at 3.9 Å resolution.
source: We present the 3.9 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the human membrane receptor guanylyl cyclase GC-C in complex with Hsp90 and its co-chaperone Cdc37, providing insight into the mechanism of Cdc37 mediated binding of GC-C to the Hsp90 regulatory complex.
evidence: The resolution and structure determination are directly stated in the abstract and supported by the cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GC-C is a membrane protein client of Hsp90-Cdc37.
source: As a membrane protein and non-kinase client of Hsp90–Cdc37, this work shows the remarkable plasticity of Cdc37 to interact with a broad array of clients with significant sequence variation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the structural data showing the complex.

claim: GC-C is a non-kinase client of Hsp90-Cdc37.
source: As a membrane protein and non-kinase client of Hsp90–Cdc37, this work shows the remarkable plasticity of Cdc37 to interact with a broad array of clients with significant sequence variation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the structural characterization showing GC-C has a pseudokinase domain.

claim: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases hijack regulatory mechanisms used for active kinases.
source: Furthermore, this work shows how membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases hijack the regulatory mechanisms used for active kinases to facilitate their regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons with kinase-Hsp90-Cdc37 complexes.

claim: cGMP is an important second messenger for signaling in mammalian physiology.
source: Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) is an important second messenger for signaling in mammalian physiology, with roles in platelet aggregation, neurotransmission, sexual arousal, gut peristalsis, bone growth, intestinal fluid secretion, lipolysis, phototransduction, cardiac hypertrophy, oocyte maturation, and blood pressure regulation (Potter, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: cGMP has roles in platelet aggregation.
source: Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) is an important second messenger for signaling in mammalian physiology, with roles in platelet aggregation, neurotransmission, sexual arousal, gut peristalsis, bone growth, intestinal fluid secretion, lipolysis, phototransduction, cardiac hypertrophy, oocyte maturation, and blood pressure regulation (Potter, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: cGMP has roles in neurotransmission.
source: Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) is an important second messenger for signaling in mammalian physiology, with roles in platelet aggregation, neurotransmission, sexual arousal, gut peristalsis, bone growth, intestinal fluid secretion, lipolysis, phototransduction, cardiac hypertrophy, oocyte maturation, and blood pressure regulation (Potter, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: cGMP has roles in blood pressure regulation.
source: Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) is an important second messenger for signaling in mammalian physiology, with roles in platelet aggregation, neurotransmission, sexual arousal, gut peristalsis, bone growth, intestinal fluid secretion, lipolysis, phototransduction, cardiac hypertrophy, oocyte maturation, and blood pressure regulation (Potter, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: cGMP is produced in response to the activation of guanylyl cyclases.
source: Largely, cGMP is produced in response to the activation of guanylyl cyclases (GC), a class of receptors that contains both heteromeric soluble receptors (α1, α2, β1, and β2 in humans) and five homomeric membrane receptors (GC-A, GC-B, GC-C, GC-E, and GC-F in humans).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about cGMP production.

claim: Humans have heteromeric soluble guanylyl cyclase receptors α1, α2, β1, and β2.
source: Largely, cGMP is produced in response to the activation of guanylyl cyclases (GC), a class of receptors that contains both heteromeric soluble receptors (α1, α2, β1, and β2 in humans) and five homomeric membrane receptors (GC-A, GC-B, GC-C, GC-E, and GC-F in humans).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about human guanylyl cyclases.

claim: Humans have five homomeric membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases: GC-A, GC-B, GC-C, GC-E, and GC-F.
source: Largely, cGMP is produced in response to the activation of guanylyl cyclases (GC), a class of receptors that contains both heteromeric soluble receptors (α1, α2, β1, and β2 in humans) and five homomeric membrane receptors (GC-A, GC-B, GC-C, GC-E, and GC-F in humans).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about human guanylyl cyclases.

claim: GC-A is also known as natriuretic peptide receptor A (NPR-A).
source: Of note are the membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases (mGC) GC-A and GC-B, also known as natriuretic peptide receptors A and B (NPR-A and NPR-B), respectively, and GC-C, all of which have been a focus of therapeutic development.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established nomenclature.

claim: GC-B is also known as natriuretic peptide receptor B (NPR-B).
source: Of note are the membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases (mGC) GC-A and GC-B, also known as natriuretic peptide receptors A and B (NPR-A and NPR-B), respectively, and GC-C, all of which have been a focus of therapeutic development.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established nomenclature.

claim: NPR-A and NPR-B regulate blood pressure in response to natriuretic peptide hormones.
source: In the case of NPR-A and B, their role in regulating blood pressure in response to natriuretic peptide hormones (ANP, BNP, and CNP) has led to the exploration of agonists for use in the treatment of cardiac failure (Kobayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Natriuretic peptide hormones include ANP, BNP, and CNP.
source: In the case of NPR-A and B, their role in regulating blood pressure in response to natriuretic peptide hormones (ANP, BNP, and CNP) has led to the exploration of agonists for use in the treatment of cardiac failure (Kobayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Linaclotide is a clinically approved laxative agonist that targets GC-C.
source: Meanwhile, GC-C is the target of clinically approved laxative agonists, linaclotide, and plecanatide (Miner, 2020; Yu and Rao, 2014), which increase intestinal fluid secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Plecanatide is a clinically approved laxative agonist that targets GC-C.
source: Meanwhile, GC-C is the target of clinically approved laxative agonists, linaclotide, and plecanatide (Miner, 2020; Yu and Rao, 2014), which increase intestinal fluid secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Linaclotide and plecanatide increase intestinal fluid secretion.
source: Meanwhile, GC-C is the target of clinically approved laxative agonists, linaclotide, and plecanatide (Miner, 2020; Yu and Rao, 2014), which increase intestinal fluid secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain (ECD).
source: These membrane receptor GCs consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain (ECD), which acts as a conformational switch to drive intracellular rearrangements to activate the receptor (He et al., 2001) a transmembrane region (TM); a kinase homology domain or pseudokinase domain (PK); a dimerization domain; and a GC domain, which acts to produce cGMP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the structural organization.

claim: The ECD of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases acts as a conformational switch to drive intracellular rearrangements to activate the receptor.
source: These membrane receptor GCs consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain (ECD), which acts as a conformational switch to drive intracellular rearrangements to activate the receptor (He et al., 2001) a transmembrane region (TM); a kinase homology domain or pseudokinase domain (PK); a dimerization domain; and a GC domain, which acts to produce cGMP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the mechanism.

claim: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases consist of a transmembrane region (TM).
source: These membrane receptor GCs consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain (ECD), which acts as a conformational switch to drive intracellular rearrangements to activate the receptor (He et al., 2001) a transmembrane region (TM); a kinase homology domain or pseudokinase domain (PK); a dimerization domain; and a GC domain, which acts to produce cGMP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the domain structure.

claim: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases consist of a kinase homology domain or pseudokinase domain (PK).
source: These membrane receptor GCs consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain (ECD), which acts as a conformational switch to drive intracellular rearrangements to activate the receptor (He et al., 2001) a transmembrane region (TM); a kinase homology domain or pseudokinase domain (PK); a dimerization domain; and a GC domain, which acts to produce cGMP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the domain structure.

claim: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases consist of a dimerization domain.
source: These membrane receptor GCs consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain (ECD), which acts as a conformational switch to drive intracellular rearrangements to activate the receptor (He et al., 2001) a transmembrane region (TM); a kinase homology domain or pseudokinase domain (PK); a dimerization domain; and a GC domain, which acts to produce cGMP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the domain structure.

claim: Membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases consist of a GC domain which acts to produce cGMP.
source: These membrane receptor GCs consist of an extracellular ligand binding domain (ECD), which acts as a conformational switch to drive intracellular rearrangements to activate the receptor (He et al., 2001) a transmembrane region (TM); a kinase homology domain or pseudokinase domain (PK); a dimerization domain; and a GC domain, which acts to produce cGMP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the domain structure and function.

claim: The PK domain of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases is involved in scaffolding and physical transduction of extracellular rearrangements to the GC domain.
source: The PK domain is largely thought to be involved in scaffolding and physical transduction of the extracellular rearrangements to the GC domain, in some respects similar to the role of the PK domain in the Janus kinases of the cytokine signaling system (Glassman et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the proposed function.

claim: The PK domains of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases are regulated through phosphorylation.
source: In addition, the PK domains of mGCs are regulated through phosphorylation (Potter and Garbers, 1992; Potter and Hunter, 1998; Vaandrager et al., 1993) and via association with heat shock proteins (Hsp) (Kumar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The PK domains of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases are regulated via association with heat shock proteins.
source: In addition, the PK domains of mGCs are regulated through phosphorylation (Potter and Garbers, 1992; Potter and Hunter, 1998; Vaandrager et al., 1993) and via association with heat shock proteins (Hsp) (Kumar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: GC-A activity can be regulated through the association of Hsp90 and the co-chaperone Cdc37.
source: It has been shown that GC-A activity can be regulated through the association of Hsp90 and the co-chaperone Cdc37 (Kumar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Cdc37 assists in the Hsp90 regulation of around 60% of active kinases.
source: The chaperone Cdc37 is known to assist in the Hsp90 regulation of around 60% of active kinases, both in soluble and membrane receptor form (Taipale et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The GC-C–Hsp90–Cdc37 complex is a hetero-tetramer formed by one monomer of GC-C bound to a dimer of Hsp90 and one Cdc37 co-chaperone.
source: The resultant GC-C–Hsp90–Cdc37 complex is a hetero-tetramer formed by one resolved monomer of the GC-C receptor bound to a dimer of Hsp90 and one Cdc37 co-chaperone (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hsp90 forms a canonical closed conformation in the GC-C–Hsp90–Cdc37 complex.
source: In this structure, the core dimer of Hsp90 forms its canonical closed conformation, while Cdc37 and the C-lobe of the GC-C PK domain asymmetrically decorate the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the structural data.

claim: The GC-C client is unfolded into the channel formed at the interface between the Hsp90 dimers.
source: The client (GC-C) is unfolded into the channel formed at the interface between the Hsp90 dimers.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the structural data.

claim: This is the first structure of a membrane protein client of Hsp90.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first structure of a membrane protein client of Hsp90 and the first structure of a non-kinase client of the Hsp90–Cdc37 regulatory system.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a novel finding of this work.

claim: This is the first structure of a non-kinase client of the Hsp90–Cdc37 regulatory system.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first structure of a membrane protein client of Hsp90 and the first structure of a non-kinase client of the Hsp90–Cdc37 regulatory system.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a novel finding of this work.

claim: The extracellular ligand binding domain was replaced with a homodimeric leucine zipper to mimic the ligand-activated geometry.
source: By replacing the ligand-responsive ECD with a homodimeric leucine zipper, we mimic the ligand-activated geometry of the ECD (He et al., 2001), while reducing complexity of the imaged complex and increasing stability (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a methodological approach with a citation and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The purified sample had a substantial portion of imaged particles with native regulatory Hsp90 and Cdc37 bound.
source: The purified sample had a substantial portion of imaged particles for which the native regulatory heat shock protein, Hsp90, and its co-chaperone, Cdc37, are bound.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the experimental observations.

claim: Cricetulus griseus HSP90β shows 99.7% identity to the human equivalent.
source: The Cricetulus griseus HSP90β and Cdc37 show remarkable sequence conservation in comparison to the human equivalents, at 99.7 and 94.2% identity, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on sequence comparison.

claim: Cricetulus griseus Cdc37 shows 94.2% identity to the human equivalent.
source: The Cricetulus griseus HSP90β and Cdc37 show remarkable sequence conservation in comparison to the human equivalents, at 99.7 and 94.2% identity, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on sequence comparison.

claim: No density is observed for the second GC-C of the dimer.
source: No density is observed for the second GC-C of the dimer, though it is sterically unlikely that an additional regulatory complex is forming on the second GC-C in a concurrent fashion, given the large size of the first Hsp90–Cdc37 and the requisite proximity of the second GC-C.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the structural data.

claim: It is sterically unlikely that an additional regulatory complex is forming on the second GC-C concurrently.
source: No density is observed for the second GC-C of the dimer, though it is sterically unlikely that an additional regulatory complex is forming on the second GC-C in a concurrent fashion, given the large size of the first Hsp90–Cdc37 and the requisite proximity of the second GC-C.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference based on structural constraints.

claim: The disruption of the native state of GC-C would likely leave GC domains out of each other's proximity, precluding their catalytic activity while Hsp90 is bound.
source: In addition, this disruption of the native state of GC-C, as observed in our structure, would likely leave GC domains out of each other's proximity, precluding their catalytic activity while Hsp90 is bound.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Cdc37 displaces the N-lobe of the pseudokinase domain of GC-C.
source: In our structures, we see that Cdc37 is displacing the N-lobe of the pseudokinase domain of GC-C, binding to the C-lobe at the N–C interface, and guiding the unfolded N-lobe into the Hsp90 dimer (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cdc37 binds to the C-lobe of GC-C at the N–C interface.
source: In our structures, we see that Cdc37 is displacing the N-lobe of the pseudokinase domain of GC-C, binding to the C-lobe at the N–C interface, and guiding the unfolded N-lobe into the Hsp90 dimer (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cdc37 guides the unfolded N-lobe into the Hsp90 dimer.
source: In our structures, we see that Cdc37 is displacing the N-lobe of the pseudokinase domain of GC-C, binding to the C-lobe at the N–C interface, and guiding the unfolded N-lobe into the Hsp90 dimer (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Cdc37–GC-C interface has a calculated mean surface area of 689 Å2.
source: The Cdc37–GC-C interface is relatively modest in size, with a calculated mean surface area of 689 Å2 (as calculated by PISA Krissinel and Henrick, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to the calculation method.

claim: The Cdc37–GC-C interface is partly driven by charge complementarity.
source: This interface is partly driven to form via charge complementarity, with positive contributions from a cluster of arginine residues on Cdc37 (R30, R32, R39) at the periphery of the interaction interface interacting with D609 and the polar residues Y580 and T586 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Arginine residues R30, R32, and R39 on Cdc37 interact with D609, Y580, and T586 on GC-C.
source: This interface is partly driven to form via charge complementarity, with positive contributions from a cluster of arginine residues on Cdc37 (R30, R32, R39) at the periphery of the interaction interface interacting with D609 and the polar residues Y580 and T586 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Cdc37–GC-C interface is largely driven by shape-complementarity.
source: Beyond this, the interface is likely largely driven via shape-complementarity, due to a minimal contribution from hydrogen bonding, salt-bridge formation, and aromatic packing contributions – in line with the ability of Cdc37 to chaperone such a diverse array of clients and client sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: GC-C residues 528–544 (VKLDTMIFGVIEYCERG) lie across the upper region of the Hsp90 CTDs.
source: Here, GC-C residues 528–544 (VKLDTMIFGVIEYCERG) lie across the upper region of the Hsp90 CTDs, which form the floor of the channel.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the structural data.

claim: The unfolded N-lobe region is relatively poorly resolved in the density.
source: The unfolded region is relatively poorly resolved in the density, with some reconstructions from earlier refinement having no resolvable density in this channel region – indicative of the low stability and high mobility of the unfolded N-lobe as it passes through this region.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the structural data.

claim: The low stability and high mobility of the unfolded N-lobe is indicated by the poorly resolved density.
source: The unfolded region is relatively poorly resolved in the density, with some reconstructions from earlier refinement having no resolvable density in this channel region – indicative of the low stability and high mobility of the unfolded N-lobe as it passes through this region.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Cdc37 associates with the C-lobe at the N-, C-lobe interface across different client–Hsp90–Cdc37 complexes.
source: Across other clients–Hsp90–Cdc37 complexes with canonical soluble kinase clients (Cdk4, RAF1, B-raf) (García-Alonso et al., 2022; Oberoi et al., 2022; Verba et al., 2016), we see a conserved role for Cdc37 in client recruitment by associating with the C-lobe at the N-, C-lobe interface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations and supported by structural comparisons shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: High levels of structural conservation are observed for Hsp90–Cdc37 across different client complexes (Cα RMSDs of 1.4–3.3 Å for Hsp90 and 1.5–2.5 Å for Cdc37).
source: In these complexes, we see high levels of structural conservation for the Hsp90–Cdc37 (Cα RMSDs of 1.4–3.3 Å for Hsp90 and 1.5–2.5 Å for Cdc37), while the client is structurally most homogenous at the interface with Cdc37, though less structurally conserved overall (Cα RMSDs of 3.5–11.6 Å).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on structural comparisons.

claim: Clients are less structurally conserved overall (Cα RMSDs of 3.5–11.6 Å) compared to Hsp90–Cdc37.
source: In these complexes, we see high levels of structural conservation for the Hsp90–Cdc37 (Cα RMSDs of 1.4–3.3 Å for Hsp90 and 1.5–2.5 Å for Cdc37), while the client is structurally most homogenous at the interface with Cdc37, though less structurally conserved overall (Cα RMSDs of 3.5–11.6 Å).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on structural comparisons.

claim: GC-C is one of the most divergent clients from a sequence perspective.
source: Perhaps unsurprisingly, GC-C is one of the most divergent of these clients from a sequence perspective (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), with sequence homology between the GC-C PK domain and the other client kinase domains ranging from 19 to 25% identity and 31 to 41% homology.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sequence homology between the GC-C PK domain and other client kinase domains ranges from 19 to 25% identity and 31 to 41% homology.
source: Perhaps unsurprisingly, GC-C is one of the most divergent of these clients from a sequence perspective (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), with sequence homology between the GC-C PK domain and the other client kinase domains ranging from 19 to 25% identity and 31 to 41% homology.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The GC-C–Hsp90–Cdc37 complex shows significant structural similarity to the mechanism that regulates soluble active kinases.
source: The present cryo-EM structure of GC-C–Hsp90–Cdc37 resolves the loading of GC-C, via its PK domain and interaction with Cdc37, to the Hsp90 core dimer (Figures 1 and 2). This complex shows significant structural similarity to the mechanism that regulates soluble active kinases (García-Alonso et al., 2022; Oberoi et al., 2022; Verba et al., 2016) and presumably membrane receptor kinases in the human proteome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: Structural and mechanistic conservation is largely driven by the co-chaperone Cdc37.
source: This structural and mechanistic conservation is largely driven by the co-chaperone Cdc37, which serves as the central binding platform for these clients by associating to the fold of the kinase (or pseudokinase in the case of mGC) domain, relatively independent of sequence identity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Cdc37 serves as the central binding platform for clients by associating to the fold of the kinase domain, relatively independent of sequence identity.
source: This structural and mechanistic conservation is largely driven by the co-chaperone Cdc37, which serves as the central binding platform for these clients by associating to the fold of the kinase (or pseudokinase in the case of mGC) domain, relatively independent of sequence identity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference based on the structural data.

claim: A model has been proposed where recruitment is largely driven by both fold complementarity and specific stability properties of the kinase fold.
source: A model whereby recruitment is largely driven by both the fold complementarity and the specific stability properties of the kinase fold has been proposed previously (Taipale et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation to support the model.

claim: In the proposed model, instability of a fully folded kinase domain results in partial unfolding of the C-lobe, leading Cdc37 to bind the partially unfolded state.
source: In this model, instability of a fully folded kinase domain results in partial unfolding of the C-lobe, leading Cdc37 to bind the partially unfolded state.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section describing a previously proposed model.

claim: The pseudokinase domains of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases have largely evolved to facilitate regulatory mechanisms for these receptors.
source: It is likely that the pseudokinase domains of mGC have largely evolved to facilitate regulatory mechanisms for these receptors, both via their phosphorylation and by hijacking the regulatory mechanisms used by active soluble and membrane receptor kinases.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Adding geldanamycin reduces the overall cGMP output of cells in response to ANP stimulation.
source: The authors showed that adding geldanamycin, an Hsp90 inhibitor, reduces the overall cGMP output of cells in response to ANP stimulation while also reducing the association of the Hsp90 to GC-A.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with reference to previous work.

claim: Geldanamycin reduces the association of Hsp90 to GC-A.
source: The authors showed that adding geldanamycin, an Hsp90 inhibitor, reduces the overall cGMP output of cells in response to ANP stimulation while also reducing the association of the Hsp90 to GC-A.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with reference to previous work.

claim: Ligand-induced activity potentiates the instability of the PK domain, which facilitates binding of the regulatory complex to 're-fold' GC-A for further catalysis.
source: While this initially may seem counterintuitive, this data fits with a model of ligand-induced activity potentiating the instability of the PK domain, which then facilitates binding of the regulatory complex to 're-fold' GC-A for further catalysis and cGMP production – in a core regulatory complex structurally similar to that which we observe for GC-C in this work (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference based on previous data and the current structural findings.

claim: PP5 is known to interact with the Hsp90–Cdc37 system and dephosphorylate Hsp90, Cdc37, and the system's kinase clients.
source: The phosphatase PP5 is known to interact with the Hsp90–Cdc37 system and dephosphorylate Hsp90, Cdc37, and the system's kinase clients (Oberoi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: PP5 has been implicated in dephosphorylation of membrane receptor guanylyl cyclases.
source: PP5 has been implicated in this role for mGC (Chinkers, 1994), though this interaction was unable to be detected by a pull-down in a second study (Kumar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The Hsp90–Cdc37 complex could refold the receptor to maintain the activity of the receptor.
source: First, the regulatory complex could refold the receptor to maintain the activity of the receptor (Figure 2—figure supplement 2i).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a possible outcome and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Hsp90–Cdc37 complex could recruit PP5 to dephosphorylate the membrane receptor guanylyl cyclase.
source: In another scenario, the Hsp90–Cdc37 complex could additionally recruit PP5 to dephosphorylate the mGC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2ii).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a possible outcome and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dephosphorylation would impair the signaling activity of GC-A, GC-B, and to some extent GC-C.
source: Particularly in the case of GC-A and GC-B, and to some extent GC-C (Potter and Garbers, 1992; Potter and Hunter, 1998; Vaandrager et al., 1993), this would impair the signaling activity of the mGC, though this could be rescued through the kinase re-association and phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The binding of the Hsp90–Cdc37 complex could result in the association of ubiquitin E3 ligases.
source: In a final scenario, the binding of the Hsp90–Cdc37 complex could result in the association of ubiquitin E3 ligases (Schopf et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 2iii), which would ubiquitinate the mGC client, leading to the removal of the receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ubiquitination of the membrane receptor guanylyl cyclase client would lead to the removal of the receptor.
source: In a final scenario, the binding of the Hsp90–Cdc37 complex could result in the association of ubiquitin E3 ligases (Schopf et al., 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 2iii), which would ubiquitinate the mGC client, leading to the removal of the receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The construct contains an HA secretion signal, FLAG peptide, linker and 3C cleavage site, GCN4 homodimeric zipper, human GC-C regions 399–1,053, a second linker and 3C cleavage site, a Protein C epitope tag, and an 8x His tag.
source: For cryo-EM studies, a construct containing an HA secretion signal (MKTIIALSYIFCLVFA), a FLAG peptide (DYKDDDD), linker and 3 C cleavage site (KGSLEVLFQGPG), GCN4 homodimeric zipper (RMKQLEDKVEELLSKNYHLENEVARLKKLVGER), human GC-C regions corresponding to the small extracellular linker region, TM, and intracellular domains (residues 399–1,053), a second linker and 3 C cleavage site (AAALEVLFQGPGAA), a Protein C epitope tag (EDQVDPRLIDGK), and an 8 x His tag were cloned into a pD649 mammalian expression vector.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the construct design.

claim: The construct contains all domains of the native GC-C, with the exception of the ECD.
source: This construct contains all domains of the native GC-C, with the exception of the ECD (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the construct design.

claim: Protein was expressed using ExpiCHO Expression System Kit.
